study_identification.author_journal_year: Itälinna et al., PLoS Computational Biology, 2023
study_identification.title: Using normative modeling and machine learning for detecting mild traumatic brain injury from magnetoencephalography data

study_characteristics.study_objective: To detect mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) from resting-state MEG measurements by using normative modeling to quantify individual patient deviations from normal variation in a large reference dataset, combined with machine learning classification to discriminate patients from healthy controls.

dataset_name.answer: Cam-CAN (Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience)

hc_age.answer: mean not provided in overall; age range 18 to 87 years; approximately 50 men and 50 women in each age decade (18-27, 28-37, 38-47, 48-57, 58-67, 68-77, 78-87 years)

hc_sex.answer: Approximately 50 men and 50 women in each age decade

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer; MNE-Python; tSSS (temporal extension of signal space separation); ICA (FastICA); dSPM inverse solution; FieldTrip for fiducial points

quality_checking_detail.answer: Subjects with missing or incomplete resting-state MEG measurements or T1-weighted MRI images were excluded, resulting in 621 subjects from nearly 700 participants. ICA was used for artifact removal (1-4 components removed based on manual inspection).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: The deviation values for control subjects were slightly below zero, probably reflecting technical differences in MEG recording sites. Authors note that multi-site calibration approaches developed for normative modeling of MRI data could be adapted to MEG data, but this was not implemented in the current study.

modeling_method.answer: Z-score based normative modeling (mean μ and standard deviation σ calculated across normative dataset subjects)

response_variable.answer: Power spectral densities (PSDs) at cortical locations across frequency range 1-40 Hz; binned into 448 cortical regions and six frequency bands (delta 1-4 Hz, theta 4-8 Hz, alpha 8-13 Hz, low beta 13-17 Hz, high beta 17-30 Hz, gamma 30-40 Hz)

predictor_effects.answer: For the full normative model, no explicit age/sex covariates were modeled; mean and SD calculated across all subjects. For age-matched models, only subjects from the same age decade were used.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses site effects to some extent by acknowledging that deviation values for control subjects were slightly below zero, reflecting technical differences between MEG recording sites. However, no formal harmonization or site effect modeling was implemented. The authors mention that multi-site calibration approaches could be adapted but were not used in this study.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: The deviation values for our control subjects were slightly below zero, probably reflecting technical differences in the MEG recording sites. To alleviate these effects, multi-site calibration approaches that have been developed for normative modeling of MRI data could be adapted to MEG data as well. Here, since the same normative model was applied to both patient and control data, we do not expect the effect on the classification results to be notable.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study employed nested cross-validation with train/test splits from the patient and control groups. Data segmentation created multiple samples per subject (7 time series per subject), and cross-validation splits ensured samples from the same subject were not in both training and validation sets.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: A nested cross-validation strategy was selected for evaluating model performance. In the inner 5-fold cross-validation loop, the best values for the regularization hyperparameters C and γ were chosen based on the best average accuracy across the folds. In the outer 7-fold loop, the model was re-trained using the chosen hyperparameters and evaluated using the independent validation set of the fold. To reduce possible bias of a single cross-validation split, the nested procedure was repeated 5 times with a different split each round, resulting in a total of 35 folds in the outer loop.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not use a completely independent held-out test set from the same domain. All evaluation was done through cross-validation on the same 25 patients and 20 controls.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: The paper describes only nested cross-validation procedures without mentioning a separate independent test cohort.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study did not validate the normative model or classifier on data from a different domain (e.g., different site, scanner, or patient cohort).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: No mention of external validation is made in the methods or results sections.

clinical_dataset.answer: Dataset from Kaltiainen et al. (2018, 2019) measured at Aalto Neuroimaging MEG Core

clinical_groups_age.answer: mTBI: mean 42 years (range 20-59 years); Control: mean 39 years (range 19-58 years)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (deviation maps calculated as Z = (X - μ) / σ where X is individual power spectrum, μ and σ are mean and SD from normative data); threshold of >2 SD used to identify abnormal theta activity

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Support Vector Machine (SVM) with radial basis function kernel for classification; nested 5×7-fold cross-validation; permutation tests (1000 iterations) for statistical significance (p<0.05); permutation feature importance to estimate feature significance; Mann-Whitney U-test to assess difference in decision function scores between patients with/without visible MRI lesions
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: mTBI patients were distinguished from healthy controls with 79.0% accuracy using normative modeling of MEG power spectra and SVM classification, with theta-band (4-8 Hz) activity providing the most significant discriminative features.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The classifier achieved 79.0% accuracy (sensitivity 91.2%, specificity 63.8%) using the full normative dataset. Theta frequency band (4-8 Hz) provided the most significant features for classification, with additional contributions from delta, alpha, and low beta bands. Most significant features were located in parietal, temporal, and occipital regions. Eight patients showed abnormal theta activity exceeding 2 SD from normative data, and these were classified with 95.0% accuracy. Only two patients were consistently misclassified; both were measured relatively late after injury (3.5-4 months) and had below-average RPQ scores. Using age-matched normative data yielded slightly lower accuracy (76.1%) compared to the full dataset. Classification without normative modeling achieved 78.6% accuracy. No significant difference was found in decision function output between patients with and without MRI-visible lesions (p=0.52).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Small clinical dataset (25 patients, 20 controls) leading to large standard deviations in performance metrics (0.15-0.32); some patients likely recovered to normal function despite earlier trauma, making 100% accuracy unrealistic; control subjects showed slightly negative deviation values reflecting technical differences between MEG recording sites; site effects were not formally addressed; artifact removal required manual inspection of ICA components; no external validation on independent cohorts; heterogeneity in mTBI mechanism, location, and symptoms makes generalization challenging; nonlinearity of SVM classifier limits direct interpretability of feature weights.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The approach demonstrated feasibility of combining normative modeling with machine learning for mTBI detection from MEG data. Individual Z-score maps enable intuitive interpretation at the patient level, which is important for clinical applicability. The framework could be adapted to other brain disorders and extended to functional connectivity measures. A future clinical application would require aggregating thousands of MEG measurements from healthy subjects across different studies, sites, and demographic variables. Automated artifact removal algorithms could enable fully automated analysis pipeline. Authors suggest limited immediate clinical application but note potential utility in identifying patients who would benefit from intervention.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is notable as one of the few applications of normative modeling to MEG/EEG data, in contrast to the majority of normative modeling studies that use structural or functional MRI. The normative dataset (Cam-CAN) is a well-characterized, publicly available dataset with nearly balanced sex distribution across age decades (18-87 years). MEG measurements were performed at 1000 Hz sampling rate with 0.03-330 Hz filtering during acquisition. Patients fulfilled ACRM criteria for mTBI: GCS 13-15 at 30 min post-accident, loss of consciousness <30 min, post-traumatic amnesia <24h. All patients were measured within 6 months post-trauma, with 19/25 measured within 2 months (subacute stage). MRI lesions were detected in 60% (15/25) of patients. Data segmentation created 7 time series per subject (200-second sliding windows with 50-second stride), yielding 315 total samples from the normative dataset. Source space had 5124 cortical locations (FreeSurfer ico-4 decimation), which were morphed to fsaverage brain and then binned into 448 cortical parcels. Dimensionality reduction from 5124×319 to 448×6 (0.16% of original size) enabled practical machine learning. Three normative modeling approaches were compared: full dataset (all ages), age-matched (same age decade), and random subset (same size as age-matched). The code to reproduce findings is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8360527 (version 1.0). Follow-up MEG recordings at 6 months were performed for 9 patients but not analyzed due to small sample size.
